written_note_arguments.docs/patchbay/link-flow-walkthrough.md:
# What happens when someone taps a Patchbay Go link

A new-contributor walkthrough of the full path a wrapped link takes, from the
chat message to the native app opening. The whole flow is stateless: every step
below is a pure function of the URL, handled by one Cloudflare Pages worker in
`src/worker.js`.

## 1. The link that gets sent

Chat apps like Telegram only linkify plain `https://` URLs, so the link someone
receives is an https address, never the raw custom scheme. Example:

    https://go.synodic.co/things/Buy%20milk

The path tail is percent-encoded by whoever built the link. The two exception
families are the bare launcher routes (`/music`, `/slack`, ...) which carry no
value, and `/raw/<base64url>` which carries an entire URI, encoded.

## 2. The request hits the worker

Tapping opens the link in the device's browser. That request lands on the
Cloudflare Pages worker (`src/worker.js`), whose `fetch` handler in the default
export is the single entry point. It reads the path and dispatches:

- `/` serves the marketing page (`dist/index.html` via the `ASSETS` binding,
  falling back to an inline usage page).
- `/key/...` goes to the E2E secret-handoff branch (KV-backed, separate flow,
  not covered in detail here).
- Everything else is a wrapped-link route.

## 3. The worker builds the native URI

Each named route is an entry in `APP_ROUTES`, which maps a short path segment
to a fixed custom-scheme prefix. The handler appends the URI-encoded path tail
to that prefix. `/things/Buy%20milk` becomes:

    things:///add?title=Buy%20milk

The same pattern holds for the three hardcoded routes:

- `/obsidian/<vault>/<path>` builds `obsidian://open?vault=...&file=...`
  (`/obs/` is an unadvertised shorthand for the same).
- `/remind/<title>` builds `x-apple-reminderkit://REMCDReminder/<title>`.
- `/cal/<date>[/<time>]` converts the date to Cocoa/CFAbsoluteTime (seconds
  since 2001-01-01, offset 978307200) and emits `calshow:<epoch>`. Note the
  comment in the source: using the Unix epoch here opens Calendar decades late,
  which was caught on-device.

Routes are safe by construction (fixed prefix plus an encoded tail), so they
skip the scheme check that `/raw` needs.

## 4. The `/raw` safety check

`/raw` takes a URI from whoever built the link, so before emitting anything the
worker base64url-decodes it and runs `isSafeScheme`. That requires a clean
`scheme:` prefix and refuses browser-privileged schemes (`javascript:`, `data:`,
`http:`, `https:`, `ws:`, and friends). This is what stops `/raw` from becoming
an open redirect or an XSS vector. Anything that fails gets a 400.

## 5. The redirect page is served

For any wrapped route the worker returns `redirectPage(appUri, message)`, a
tiny self-contained HTML page. It shows a spinner, a friendly line like
"Opening Things", a manual "tap here if nothing happened" link, and then fires
two redundant handoffs to the custom scheme:

1. A meta refresh in the head: `http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=<appUri>"`.
2. An inline script: `window.location.href = <appUri>`.

The redundancy matters because some browsers ignore one mechanism or the other.
All interpolated values go through `escapeHtml` / `escapeAttr` /
`jsStringLiteral`, so nothing from the URL can break out of the page (the
`jsStringLiteral` helper in particular neutralizes `</script>` and Unicode line
separators).

## 6. The browser hands off to the OS

The browser navigates to the custom scheme URI. Browsers do not understand
schemes like `things://` or `calshow:`, so they pass the URI to the operating
system, which looks up which installed app registered that scheme and launches
it with the URI as the payload. That is why the handoff works in the browser
but not in the chat app: chat apps only linkify https, while browsers are the
one hop where custom schemes are allowed.

## 7. If the app is missing

If no app is registered for the scheme, the OS shows an error or silently does
nothing and the redirect page simply stays on screen. There is no error the
worker could catch here — this is platform behavior, not the worker's. The
worker's fallback text on the page says so: the link only works where the app
is installed.

## Where each piece lives

- `src/worker.js` — the entire relay: routes, URI building, `/raw` check,
  redirect page, key handoff.
- `website/index.html` — the marketing/landing page (built into `dist/`).
- `clients/patchbay_key.py` — the reference agent client for the `/key`
  secret-handoff flow.
- `wrangler.toml` / `DEPLOYING.md` — deployment, routes bound to a domain.
